L32: # The Group Structure of Pivot and Loop Complementation on Graphs and Set Systems
L33: 
L34: Robert Brijder Email: robert.brijder@uhasselt.be Corresponding author: Corresponding author Address: Hasselt University and Transnational University of Limburg, Belgium    Hendrik Jan Hoogeboom Address: Leiden Institute of Advanced Computer Science,
L35: Leiden University, The Netherlands
L36: ###### Abstract
L37: We study the interplay between principal pivot transform (pivot) and loop complementation for graphs. This is done by generalizing loop complementation (in addition to pivot) to set systems. We show that the operations together, when restricted to single vertices, form the permutation group $S_{3}$. This leads, e.g., to a normal form for sequences of pivots and loop complementation on graphs.
L38: The results have consequences for the operations of local complementation and edge complementation on simple graphs: an alternative proof of a classic result involving local and edge complementation is obtained, and the effect of sequences of local complementations on simple graphs is characterized.
L39: ###### Keywords:
L40: 
L41: local complementation , principal pivot transform , circle graph , interlace polynomial , delta-matroid , algebraic graph theory
L42: ## 1 Introduction
L43: Principal pivot transform (PPT, or simply pivot), due to Tucker [cite20†21 ], partially inverts a given matrix. Its definition is originally motivated by the extensively studied linear complementarity problem [cite21†11 ]. However, there are many other application areas for PPT, see [cite22†20 ] for an overview. We consider pivots on graphs where loops are allowed (i.e., symmetric matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$).
L44: It is shown by Bouchet [cite23†4 ] that, in this case, the pivot operation satisfies an equivalent definition in terms of set systems (more specifically, in terms of delta-matroids due to a specific exchange axiom that they fulfill).
L45: Pivot operations on graphs (where loops are allowed) can be decomposed into two types of elementary pivots: local complementation and edge complementation. The names “local complementation” and “edge complementation” are due to similar operations on simple graphs. Local complementation on simple graphs has originally been considered in [cite24†16 ] and edge complementation has subsequently been defined in terms of local complementation in [cite25†5 ].
L46: There these operations were motivated by circle graphs (or overlap graphs), where local and edge complementation model natural transformations on the underlying interval segments (or, equivalently, on Euler tours within a 4-regular graph). Many other application areas have since been identified.
L47: For example, local complementation on simple graphs retains the entanglement of the corresponding graph states in quantum computing [cite26†22 ], and this operation is of main interest in relation to rank-width in the vertex-minor project initiated in [cite27†17 ]. Moreover, edge complementation is fundamentally related to the interlace polynomial [cite28†2 , cite29†3 , cite30†1 ], the definition of which is motivated by the computation of the number of $k$-component circuit partitions in a graph.
L48: Elementary pivots on graphs naturally appear in the formal study of gene assembly in ciliates [cite31†12 , cite32†8 ] (a research area of computational biology).
L49: Surprisingly, the similarity between local and edge complementation for simple graphs on the one hand and pivots on matrices (or graphs) on the other hand has been largely unnoticed (although it is observed in [cite33†13 ]), and as a result they have been studied almost independently.
L50: In this paper we consider the interplay between pivots and loop complementation (flipping the existence of loops for a given set of vertices) on graphs. By generalizing loop complementation to set systems, we obtain a common viewpoint for the two operations: pivots and loop complementations are elements of order $2$ (i.e., involutions) in the permutation group $S_{3}$ (by restricting to single vertices). We find that the dual pivot from [cite34†9 ] corresponds to the third element of order $2$ in $S_{3}$.
L51: We obtain a normal form for sequences of pivots and loop complementations on graphs. As a consequence a number of results for local and edge complementations on simple graphs are obtained including an alternative proof of a classic result [cite25†5 ] relating local and edge complementation (see Proposition cite35†23 ). Finally we characterize the effect of sequences of local complementations on simple graphs.
L52: In this way we find that, surprisingly, loops are the key to fully understand local and edge complementation on simple (i.e., loopless) graphs, as they bridge the gap in the definitions of local and edge complementation for graphs on the one hand and simple graphs on the other.
L53: An extended abstract of this paper containing selected results without proofs was presented at TAMC 2010 [cite36†10 ].
L54: ## 2 Notation and Terminology
L55: In this paper matrix computations (except for the first part of Section cite8†3 ) will be over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$, the field consisting of two elements. We will often consider this field as the Booleans, and its operations addition and multiplication are as such equal to the logical exclusive-or and logical conjunction, which are denoted by $\oplus$ and $\land$ respectively. These operations carry over to sets, e.g., for sets $A,B\subseteq V$ and $x\in V$, $x\in A\oplus B$ iff $(x\in A)\oplus(x\in B)$.
L56: A set system (over $V$) is an ordered pair $M=(V,D)$ with $V$ a finite set and $D$ a family of subsets of $V$. We write simply $Y\in M$ to denote $Y\in D$. For $X\subseteq V$, $X$ is minimal (maximal, resp.) in $D$ w.r.t. inclusion iff both $X\in D$ and $Y\not\in D$ for every $Y\subset X$ ($Y\supset X$, resp.). The set of minimal (maximal, resp.) elements of $D$ (w.r.t. inclusion) is denoted by $\min(D)$ ($\max(D)$, resp.). Moreover, we write $\min(M)=\min(D)$ and $\max(M)=\max(D)$.
L57: For a $V\times V$-matrix $A$ (the columns and rows of $A$ are indexed by finite set $V$) and $X\subseteq V$, $A[X]$ denotes the principal submatrix of $A$ w.r.t. $X$, i.e., the $X\times X$-matrix obtained from $A$ by restricting to rows and columns in $X$.
L58: We consider undirected graphs without parallel edges, however we do allow loops. For graph $G=(V,E)$ we use $V(G)$ and $E(G)$ to denote its set of vertices $V$ and set of edges $E$, respectively, where for $x\in V$, $\{x\}\in E$ iff $x$ has a loop. For $X\subseteq V$, we denote the subgraph of $G$ induced by $X$ as $G[X]$.
L59: With a graph $G$ one associates its adjacency matrix $A(G)$, which is a $V\times V$-matrix $\left(a_{u,v}\right)$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ with $a_{u,v}=1$ iff $\{u,v\}\in E$ (we have $a_{u,u}=1$ iff $\{u\}\in E$). In this way, the family of graphs with vertex set $V$ corresponds precisely to the family of symmetric $V\times V$-matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$.
L60: Therefore we often make no distinction between a graph and its matrix, so, e.g., by the determinant of graph $G$, denoted $\det G$, we will mean the determinant $\det A(G)$ of its adjacency matrix (computed over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$). By convention, $\det(G[\varnothing])=1$.
L61: For graph $G$, the loop complementation operation on a set of vertices $X\subseteq V$, denoted by $G+X$, removes loops from the vertices of $X$ when present in $G$ and adds loops to vertices of $X$ when not present in $G$. Hence the adjacency matrix of $G+X$ is obtained from $A(G)$ by adding $1$ to each diagonal element $a_{xx}$, $x\in X$, of $A(G)$. Clearly, $(G+X)+Y=G+(X\oplus Y)$ for $X,Y\subseteq V$.

L88: #### Set Systems

L46: ###### Abstract.
L47: 
L48: We define a class of trim metric spaces and show that each finite metric space is isometric to the leaf space of a metric forest with trim base.
L49: 
L50: ###### 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
L51: 
L52: 54E35
L53: ## 1. Introduction
L54: Finite metric spaces naturally arise in mathematics, informatics and phylogenetics, see [cite26†DHM ], [cite27†Li ], [cite28†SS ]. We introduce here a class of trim metric spaces and show that every finite metric space is the leaf space of a metric forest with trim base. We use the language of pseudometrics and begin by recalling the relevant terminology. A pseudometric space is a pair consisting of a set $X$ and a mapping $d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ (the pseudometric) such that for all $x,y,z\in X$,
L55:  | $$d(x,x)=0,\quad d(x,y)=d(y,x)\geq 0,\quad d(x,y)+d(y,z)\geq d(x,z).$$  |
L56: 
L57: Pseudometric spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X^{\prime},d^{\prime})$ are isometric if there is a bijection $X\to X^{\prime}$ carrying $d$ to $d^{\prime}$. A map $q:X\to X^{\prime}$ is non-expansive if $d(x,y)\geq d^{\prime}(q(x),q(y))$ for all $x,y\in X$. A metric space is a pseudometric space $(X,d)$ such that $d(x,y)>0$ for all distinct $x,y\in X$ (and then $d$ is a metric).
L58: Given points $x,y,z$ of a pseudometric space $(X,d)$, we say following K. Menger [cite29†Me ] that $x$ lies between $y$ and $z$ if $x,y,z$ are pairwise distinct and
L59: 
L60: (1.0.1)  |  | $$d(x,y)+d(x,z)=d(y,z).$$  |
L61: We say that a finite pseudometric space $(X,d)$ is trim if either $\operatorname{card}(X)\leq 1$ or every point of $X$ lies between two other points of $X$ (that is for each $x\in X$, there are distinct $y,z\in X\setminus\{x\}$ satisfying (cite30†1.0.1 )). It is easy to give examples of trim pseudometric spaces. For instance, any finite set with $\geq 3$ elements and zero pseudometric $d=0$ is trim. On the other hand, the class of trim metric spaces is quite narrow.
L62: In particular, there are no trim metric spaces having just two points or three points. A finite subset of a Euclidean space with $\geq 2$ points and with the induced metric cannot be trim. Indeed, such a subset must contain a pair of points lying at the maximal distance; these points cannot lie between other points of the subset. Consequently, trim finite metric spaces having more than one point do not isometrically embed into Euclidean spaces.
L63: We give here three examples of trim metric spaces:
L64: 
L65: (1) the set of words of a fixed finite length $\geq 2$ in a given finite alphabet with the Hamming distance defined as the number of positions at which the letters of two words differ;
L66: 
L67: (2) a subset of a Euclidean circle $C\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}$ meeting each half-circle in $C$ in at least three points; here the distance between points is the length of the shorter arc in $C$ connecting these points;
L68: (3) the 4-point metric space $\{a,b,c,e\}$ with metric $d$ defined by
L69: 
L70:  | $$d(a,b)=d(c,e)=r,\,\,\,\,d(a,c)=d(b,e)=s,\,\,\,\,d(a,e)=d(b,c)=r+s,$$  |
L71: 
L72: where $r,s>0$ are real numbers. This is a special case of Example 2 arising from 4-point subsets of $C$ formed by two pairs of diametrically opposite points.
L73: Our main construction derives from any finite pseudometric space $X$ a trim finite metric space $c(X)$, called the trim core of $X$, and a surjective non-expansive map $q_{X}:X\to c(X)$. The construction of $c(X)$ and $q_{X}$ is functorial: each isometry of finite pseudometric spaces $\varphi:X\to X^{\prime}$ induces an isometry $c(\varphi):c(X)\to c(X^{\prime})$ such that $q_{X^{\prime}}\varphi=c(\varphi)\,q_{X}:X\to c(X^{\prime})$.
L74: If $X$ is a trim metric space, then $c(X)=X$ and $q_{X}=\operatorname{id}_{X}$.
L75: Pseudometric spaces whose trim core is a point can be described in terms of trees. By a tree, we mean a metric tree, i.e., a connected graph without cycles whose edges are endowed with non-negative real numbers called the lengths. The set of vertices of a tree $\tau$ carries the path pseudometric $d_{\tau}$: the distance between any vertices of $\tau$ is the sum of the lengths of the edges of $\tau$ forming the shortest path between these vertices.
L76: The leaf space of a tree $\tau$ is the set of all degree 1 vertices of $\tau$ together with the pseudometric $d_{\tau}$ restricted to this set. A tree is finite if it has a finite number of vertices and edges.
L77: ###### Theorem 1.1.
L78: 
L79: The trim core of a finite pseudometric space $X$ is a point if and only if $\operatorname{card}(X)=1$ or $X$ is isometric to the leaf space of a finite tree.
L80: Besides the trim core, each finite pseudometric space determines a bunch of rooted trees or, more precisely, a metric forest. A rooted tree is a tree having at least one edge and a distinguished vertex $\ast$, the root. A leaf of a rooted tree $\tau$ is a vertex of $\tau$ which is distinct from $\ast$ and has degree 1. The set of all leaves of $\tau$ is denoted by $\partial\tau$; the pseudometric space $({\partial\tau},d_{\tau}|_{{\partial\tau}})$ is the leaf space of $\tau$.
L81: A metric forest $\zeta$ consists of a metric space $B=(B,d_{B})$ called the base and a family of rooted trees $(\zeta_{a},\ast_{a})_{a\in B}$ called the components. By vertices, edges and leaves of $\zeta$ we mean the vertices, edges and leaves of the components of $\zeta$. The leaf space of $\zeta$ is the disjoint union ${\partial\zeta}=\amalg_{a\in B}\,{\partial\zeta_{a}}$ with the following pseudometric $d_{\zeta}$: for any $x\in{\partial\zeta_{a}},y\in{\partial\zeta_{b}}$ with $a,b\in B$,
L82: (1.0.2)  |  | $$d_{\zeta}(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}d_{\zeta_{a}}(x,y)\quad{\text{if}}\,\,a=b,\\
L83: d_{\zeta_{a}}(x,\ast_{a})+d_{B}(a,b)+d_{\zeta_{b}}(y,\ast_{b})\quad{\text{if}}\,\,a\neq b.\end{array}\right.$$  |
L84: 
L85: For example, any metric space $B$ determines a metric forest $\{[0,1]_{a}\}_{a\in B}$ where $[0,1]_{a}$ is a copy of the segment $[0,1]$ with vertices $0,1$, root $0$, and zero length of the only edge. The leaf space of this metric forest is isometric to $B$.
L86: A metric forest is finite if its base is a finite metric space and all its components are finite rooted trees.
L87: ###### Theorem 1.2.
L88: 
L89: Any finite pseudometric space $X$ determines (in a canonical way) a finite metric forest with leaf space $X$ and base $c(X)$.
L90: 
L91: For finite pseudometric spaces $X,Y$, we write $X\geq Y$ if there is a finite metric forest with leaf space $X$ and base $Y$. Theorem cite31†1.2 implies that $X\geq c(X)$ for any finite pseudometric space $X$. We now explain that this property may be used to characterize $c(X)$ at least up to isometry.
L92: ###### Theorem 1.3.
L93: 
L94: For any finite metric forest $\zeta$ with trim base $B$, we have $c(\partial\zeta)=B$ (up to isometry).
L95: 
L96: ###### Corollary 1.4.
L97: 
L98: If a finite pseudometric space $X$ and a trim finite metric space $B$ satisfy $X\geq B$, then $c(X)=B$ (up to isometry).
L99: 
L100: We say that two finite pseudometric spaces are trim equivalent if their trim cores are isometric. The next theorem generalizes Theorem cite32†1.3 to arbitrary finite metric forests.
L101: ###### Theorem 1.5.
L102: 
L103: The leaf space and the base of any finite metric forest are trim equivalent to each other.
L104: 
L105: We define the trim core in Section cite7†2 and prove Theorems cite33†1.1 –cite34†1.5 in Sections cite14†3 –cite20†5 .

L107: ## 2. Trimming and the trim core
L108: ### 2.1. Trim spaces
L109: 
L110: Given a set $X$ and a map $d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$, we will use the same symbol $d$ for the map $X\times X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by
L111: 
L112:  | $$d(x,y,z)=\frac{d(x,y)+d(x,z)-d(y,z)}{2}$$  |
L113: for all $x,y,z\in X$. We derive from any pseudometric $d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ a function $\underline{d}:X\to\mathbb{R}$: if $X$ has only one point, then $\underline{d}=0$; if $X$ has two points $x,y$, then $\underline{d}(x)=\underline{d}(y)=d(x,y)/2$; if $X$ has $\geq 3$ points, then for all $x\in X$,
L114: 
L115:  | $${\underline{d}}(x)=\inf_{y,z\in X\setminus\{x\},y\neq z}d(x,y,z)\geq 0.$$  |
L116: We say that a pseudometric space $(X,d)$ is trim if $\underline{d}=0$. It is clear that for finite $X$ this definition is equivalent to the one in the introduction.
L117: ### 2.2. Metric quotient
L118: Any pseudometric space $(X,d)$ determines a metric space $(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{d})$ called the metric quotient of $(X,d)$. Here $\widetilde{X}=X/{\sim_{d}}$ where $\sim_{d}$ is the equivalence relation on $X$ defined by $x\sim_{d}y$ if $d(x,y)=0$ for $x,y\in X$. The metric $\widetilde{d}$ in $\widetilde{X}$ is uniquely defined by ${\widetilde{d}}(\widetilde{x},\widetilde{y})=d(x,y)$ where $x,y$ are any points of $X$ and $\widetilde{x},\widetilde{y}\in\widetilde{X}$ are their equivalence classes.
L119: The metric quotient of a trim pseudometric space may be non-trim. For example, let $X=\{x,y,a,b\}$ and let the distance between any point of the set $\{x,y\}$ with any point of $\{a,b\}$ be 1 while all the other distances between points of $X$ be $0$. The resulting pseudometric space $X$ is trim (for instance, $x$ lies between $y$ and $a$). However, the metric space $\widetilde{X}$ has two points and is not trim.
L120: ### 2.3. Drift
L121: 
L122: Given a set $X$, a map $d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ and a function $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$, we define a map $d^{f}:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ by the following rule: for any $x,y\in X$,
L123: 
L124:  | $$d^{f}(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0\quad{\text{if}}\,\,x=y,\\
L125: d(x,y)+f(x)+f(y)\quad{\text{if}}\,\,x\neq y.\end{array}\right.$$  |
L126: 
L127: We say that $d^{f}$ is obtained from $d$ by a drift. The idea here is that each point of $X$ is carried away from all the other points by the distance $f(x)$.
L128: ###### Lemma 2.1.
L129: 
L130: If $(X,d)$ is a pseudometric space and $f:X\to\mathbb{R}$ is a function such that $f(x)\geq-{\underline{d}}(x)$ for all $x\in X$, then $(X,{d^{f}})$ is a pseudometric space. Moreover, if $\operatorname{card}(X)\geq 3$ or $\operatorname{card}(X)=2$ and $f$ is a constant function, then $\underline{d^{f}}=\underline{d}+f$.
L131: ###### Proof.
L132: 
L133: We first prove that for any distinct $x,y\in X$,
L134: 
L135: (2.3.1)  |  | $${\underline{d}}(x)+{\underline{d}}(y)\leq d(x,y).$$  |
L136: 
L137: If $X=\{x,y\}$, then (cite35†2.3.1 ) follows from the definition of $\underline{d}$. If $\operatorname{card}(X)\geq 3$, we pick any $z\in X\setminus\{x,y\}$. Then ${\underline{d}}(x)\leq{d(x,y,z)}$ and ${\underline{d}}(y)\leq d(y,x,z)$. So,
L138: 
L139:  | $${\underline{d}}(x)+{\underline{d}}(y)\leq d(x,y,z)+d(y,x,z)=(d(x,y)+d(y,x))/{2}=d(x,y).$$  |
L140: We now check that ${d^{f}}:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ is a pseudometric. Clearly, ${d^{f}}$ is symmetric and, by definition, ${d^{f}}(x,x)=0$ for all $x\in X$. Formula (cite35†2.3.1 ) and the assumptions on $f$ imply that for any distinct $x,y\in X$,
L141: 
L142:  | $${d^{f}}(x,y)=d(x,y)+f(x)+f(y)\geq{\underline{d}}(x)+f(x)+{\underline{d}}(y)+f(y)\geq 0.$$  |
L143: 
L144: The triangle inequality for $d^{f}$ may be rewritten as $d^{f}(x,y,z)\geq 0$ for any $x,y,z\in X$. If $x,y,z$ are pairwise distinct, then
L145: (2.3.2)  |  | $$d^{f}(x,y,z)=d(x,y,z)+f(x).$$  |
L146: 
L147: Hence $d^{f}(x,y,z)\geq{\underline{d}}(x)+f(x)\geq 0$. If $x=y$ or $x=z$, then $d^{f}(x,y,z)=0$; if $y=z$, then $d^{f}(x,y,z)=d^{f}(x,y)\geq 0$.
L148: 
L149: The equality $\underline{d^{f}}=\underline{d}+f$ follows from (cite36†2.3.2 ) if $\operatorname{card}(X)\geq 3$ and from the definitions if $\operatorname{card}(X)=2$ and $f=const$. ∎
L150: ### 2.4. Trimming
L151: 
L152: Given a pseudometric space $(X,d)$, we can apply Lemma cite37†2.1 to $f=-\underline{d}:X\to\mathbb{R}$. This gives a pseudometric in $X$ denoted $d^{\bullet}$. By definition, for any $x,y\in X$,
L153: 
L154: (2.4.1)  |  | $$d^{\bullet}(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0\quad{\text{if}}\,\,x=y,\\
L155: d(x,y)-\underline{d}(x)-\underline{d}(y)\quad{\text{if}}\,\,x\neq y.\end{array}\right.$$  |
L156: Lemma cite37†2.1 implies that $\underline{d^{\bullet}}=0$ so that $(X,d^{\bullet})$ is a trim pseudometric space. Let $t(X)=(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{d^{\bullet}})$ be its metric quotient. We say that $t(X)$ is obtained from $(X,d)$ by trimming. Note that the metric space $t(X)$ may be non-trim.
L157: By the definition of the metric quotient, $\widetilde{X}=X/{\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}$ and the projection $p_{X}:X\to\widetilde{X}$ is a non-expansive surjection. It is bijective if and only if ${d^{\bullet}}$ is a metric. In this case, $\widetilde{X}=X$, $\widetilde{d^{\bullet}}={d^{\bullet}}$ and $t(X)$ is a trim metric space.
L158: Though it is not used in the sequel, we compute the equivalence relation ${\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}$ in $X$ directly from $d$. Note first that if $1\leq\operatorname{card}(X)\leq 3$, then all elements of $X$ are related by ${\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}$ and $t(X)=\{pt\}$ (exercise).
L159: ###### Lemma 2.2.
L160: 
L161: Suppose that $\operatorname{card}(X)\geq 3$. Two distinct elements $x,y\in X$ are related by ${\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}$ if and only if for any distinct $x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime}\in X\setminus\{x\}$ and any distinct $y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime}\in X\setminus\{y\}$, we have
L162: 
L163:  | $$2d(x,y)+d(x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime})+d(y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime})\leq d(x,x^{\prime})+d(x,x^{\prime\prime})+d(y,y^{\prime})+d(y,y^{\prime\prime}).$$  |
L164: ###### Proof.
L165: 
L166: It follows from the definitions that
L167: 
L168:  | $$x{\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}y\Longleftrightarrow d^{\bullet}(x,y)=0\Longleftrightarrow d(x,y)=\underline{d}(x)+\underline{d}(y).$$  |
L169: 
L170: By (cite35†2.3.1 ), the latter equality holds iff $d(x,y)\leq\underline{d}(x)+\underline{d}(y)$. Recall that
L171:  | $${\underline{d}}(x)=\inf_{x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime}\in X\setminus\{x\},x^{\prime}\neq x^{\prime\prime}}d(x,x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime})\,\,\,{\text{and}}\,\,\,{\underline{d}}(y)=\inf_{y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime}\in X\setminus\{y\},y^{\prime}\neq y^{\prime\prime}}d(y,y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime}).$$  |
L172: 
L173: Thus,
L174: 
L175:  | $$x{\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}y\Longleftrightarrow d(x,y)\leq d(x,x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime})+d(y,y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime})$$  |
L176: for any distinct $x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime}\in X\setminus\{x\}$ and distinct $y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime}\in X\setminus\{y\}$. Substituting here the defining expression of the function $d:X\times X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$, we obtain the claim of the lemma. ∎
L177: ### 2.5. The trim core
L178: 
L179: Starting from a pseudometric space $X$ and iterating the trimming, we obtain metric spaces $\{t^{n}(X)\}_{n\geq 1}$ and non-expansive surjections
L180: 
L181: (2.5.1)  |  | $$X=t^{0}(X)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p_{0}}}{{\longrightarrow}}t(X)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}}t^{2}(X)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\cdots$$  |
L182: where $p_{n}=p_{t^{n}(X)}$ for all $n\geq 0$. We say that $X$ has finite height if $t^{n}(X)$ is a trim metric space for some $n\geq 0$. The minimal such $n$ is the height of $X$ and the corresponding metric space $c(X)=t^{n}(X)$ is the trim core of $X$. For a pseudometric space $X$ of finite height $n\geq 0$, the map
L183: 
L184:  | $$q_{X}=p_{n-1}\circ\cdots p_{1}\circ p_{0}:X\to t^{n}(X)=c(X)$$  |
L185: is a non-expansive surjection while the maps $\{p_{m}\}_{m\geq n}$ are isometries. Note that $c(t(X))=c(X)$ and, if $n\geq 1$, then $height(t(X))=n-1$. Clearly, $height(X)=0$ if and only if $X$ is a trim metric space and then $c(X)=t(X)=X$.
L186: 
L187: These definitions and results apply, in particular, to any finite pseudometric space $X$. Indeed, for $N=\operatorname{card}(X)$, at least one of the surjections $p_{0},p_{1},...,p_{N-1}$ in (cite38†2.5.1 ) must be bijective. Hence, $height(X)\leq N$ and $c(X)=t^{N}(X)$.
L188: ### 2.6. Remarks
L189: 
L190: 1. If a pseudometric space $(X,d)$ has $\geq 3$ points, then the function ${\underline{d}}:X\to\mathbb{R}$ can be computed by a slightly shorter formula
L191: 
L192:  | $${\underline{d}}(x)=\inf_{y,z\in X\setminus\{x\}}d(x,y,z)$$  |
L193: 
L194: for any $x\in X$. To deduce this from the definition of $\underline{d}$, it suffices to note that by (cite35†2.3.1 ), we have ${\underline{d}}(x)\leq d(x,y)=d(x,y,y)$ for all $y\in X\setminus\{x\}$.
L195: 2. The maps (cite38†2.5.1 ) induce a sequence of equivalence relations $\{\sim_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}$ in any pseudometric space $(X,d)$: points of $X$ are related by $\sim_{n}$ if their images in $t^{n}(X)$ are equal. Clearly, ${\sim_{1}}={\sim_{d^{\bullet}}}$ and $x\sim_{n}y\Longrightarrow x\sim_{n+1}y$ for all $x,y\in X$.
L196: 3. For any $X,d,f$ as in Lemma cite37†2.1 , the pseudometric space $X^{f}=(X,d^{f})$ satisfies $(d^{f})^{\bullet}=d^{\bullet}:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$. Therefore $t(X^{f})=t(X)$, i.e., the trimming turns $X$ and $X^{f}$ into the same metric space. Consequently, if $X$ has a finite height, then so does $X^{f}$ and $c(X^{f})=c(X)$.
L197: 4. Consider a finite set $X$ and a map $h:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $h(x,y)=h(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in X$. For $r\in\mathbb{R}$, we define a map $h_{r}:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ by
L198: 
L199:  | $$h_{r}(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0\quad{\text{if}}\,\,x=y,\\
L200: h(x,y)+r\quad{\text{if}}\,\,x\neq y.\end{array}\right.$$  |

L499: ### 4.1 The classical tight span

L501: Here we show that the Isbell’s tight span of a classical metric space is contained in the Isbell completion of the metic space.
L502: ###### Theorem 6.
L503: 
L504: If $\mathsf{X}$ is a classical metric space then the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})$ is (isometric to) the maximal classical metric space inside the generalized metric space $I(\mathsf{X})$ which contains the image of $\mathsf{X}$.
L505: ###### Proof.

L507: In Section cite8†2.1 the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})\subset\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$ is characterized by
L508: 
L509:  | $$T(\mathsf{X})=\bigl\{f\in\widehat{\mathsf{X}}\bigm|f(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathsf{X}}(\dd(x,y)\mminus f(y))\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathsf{X}\bigr\}.$$  |

L514: ### 4.2 The directed tight span of Hirai and Koichi
L515: For a finite generalized metric space with no infinite distances, Hirai and Koichi [cite65†9 ] defined a ‘tight span’ which they denoted $T_{\mu}$, where $\mu$ was the generalized metric. For a generalized metric space $X$ we will use the notation $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{HK}}(X)$ and refer to it as the Hirai-Koichi tight span. L517: Let $P(X)$ be the set of pairs $(f,g)$ of functions $f,g\colon X\to[0,\infty]$ such that

L519:  | $$f(x)+g(y)\geq\dd(x,y)\quad\text{for all }x,y\in X.$$  |

L204: ## \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1pt2 \sectionrule 3ex0pt-1ex1ptIsbell’s tight span in category-theoretic language
L205: In this section we state Isbell’s original definition of the tight span, his ‘injective envelope’, and then reformulate it in a fashion amenable to a category theoretic analysis. We then compare the two approaches in some simple examples, seeing that the two approaches, but not the final answers, are indeed somewhat different. Throughout this section we use a sans serif symbol such as $\mathsf{X}$ to denote a classical metric space.
L206: Whilst in the literature the tight span and the injective envelope are used to mean the same thing, here I will use the terminology to distinguish two isometric metric spaces.
L207: ### 2.1 Two definitions of the tight span
L208: 
L209: Isbell, in his 1964 paper [cite56†10 ], constructs for a classical metric space $\mathsf{X}$ the ‘injective envelope’ $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ in the following way. Firstly define $\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ the aim of $\mathsf{X}$ by $f\in\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ if $f$ is a real-valued function on $\mathsf{X}$ which satisfies
L210: 
L211:  | $$f(x)+f(y)\geq\dd(x,y)\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathsf{X}.$$  |
L212: A function $f\in\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ is pointwise-minimal if whenever $g\in\Aim(\mathsf{X})$ satisfies $g(x)\leq f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathsf{X}$ then $g=f$. We then define the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ to be the classical metric space of pointwise-minimal functions in $\Aim(\mathsf{X})$, with the metric on $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ given by
L213: 
L214:  | $$\dd_{\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})}(f,g)=\sup_{x\in\mathsf{X}}|f(x)-g(x)|.$$  |
L215: That is the standard definition of the injective envelope or tight span, however, we can characterize it in the following way which is amenable to the category theoretic approach. Let the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})\subset\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$ be the subset of presheaves on $\mathsf{X}$ such that a presheaf $f\colon\mathsf{X}\to[0,\infty]$ is in $T(\mathsf{X})$ if
L216: 
L217:  | $$f(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathfrak{\mathsf{X}}}\bigl(\dd(x,y)\mminus f(y)\bigr)\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathsf{X}.$$  |
L218: The metric on $T(\mathsf{X})$ is induced from the generalized metric on $\widehat{\mathsf{X}}$. A calculation shows that the metric on $T(\mathsf{X})$ is actually symmetric.
L219: These two definitions are equivalent in that there is a canonical isomorphism of metric spaces $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})\cong T(\mathsf{X})$: indeed, in some sense, they have the same set of points; however, they are defined as subspaces of different spaces. The details of the proof that they are isometric are given by Dress [cite57†6 ]; the subtle part is showing that the metrics actually agree. Theorem cite66†7 generalizes this result and the proof given there is a generalization of Dress’ proof.
L220: Before comparing the injective envelope $\mathcal{E}(\mathsf{X})$ and the tight span $T(\mathsf{X})$ in some examples, it is worth noting two things about the tight span. The first thing is that $\mathsf{X}$ maps isometrically in to its tight-span $T(\mathsf{X})$ via the Yoneda map:
L221: 
L222:  | $$\Yoneda\colon\mathsf{X}\to T(\mathsf{X});\qquad x\mapsto\dd({-},x).$$  |

L224: The supremum condition (cite70†2.1 ) on $f$ is saying that “for every point $x\in\mathsf{X}$ the point $p_{f}$ is arbitrarily close to being on a geodesic from $x$ to another point”; in other terms, for all $\varepsilon\geq 0$ there is a $y$ such that $\dd(x,p_{f})+\dd(p_{f},y)\leq d(x,y)+\varepsilon$. This is expressing the minimality of the tight-span $T(\mathsf{X})$, saying that the points of $T(\mathsf{X})$ must ‘lie between’ the points of $\mathsf{X}$.

L220: ## 6 Compositions of Loop Complementation and Pivot
L221: 
L222: In this section we study sequences of loop complementation and pivot operations. As we may consider both operations as vertex flips, we obtain in a straightforward way general equalities involving loop complementation and pivot.

L224: ###### Theorem 11
L225: 
L226: Let $M$ be a set system over $V$ and $X\subseteq V$. Then $M+X*X+X=M*X+X*X$.
L227: ###### Proof 4
L228: 
L229: In group $S_{3}$ we have $aba=bab=c$. Hence $\alpha_{+}\alpha_{*}\alpha_{+}=\alpha_{*}\alpha_{+}\alpha_{*}$. Now by Lemma cite46†5 , we have $M+\{j\}*\{j\}+\{j\}=M*\{j\}+\{j\}*\{j\}$ for any $j\in V$. By the commutative property of vertex flip in Lemma cite46†5 , this can be generalized to sets $X\subseteq V$, and hence we obtain the desired result. ∎
L230: Let us denote $\alpha_{\mathop{\bar{*}}}=\alpha_{+}\alpha_{*}\alpha_{+}$ and denote, for $X\subseteq V$, $M\alpha^{X}_{\mathop{\bar{*}}}$ by $M\mathop{\bar{*}}X$. We will call the $\mathop{\bar{*}}$ operation the dual pivot. As $\alpha_{+}$ is of order $2$, we have, similar to the pivot operation and loop complementation, $(M\mathop{\bar{*}}X)\mathop{\bar{*}}Y=M\mathop{\bar{*}}(X\oplus Y)$.
L231: The dual pivot together with pivot and loop complementation correspond precisely to the elements of order $2$ in $S_{3}$.

L233: ###### Theorem 12
L234: 
L235: Let $M$ be a set system over $V$, and let $\varphi$ be any sequence of pivot and loop complementation operations on elements in $V$. We have that $M\varphi=M+X*Y+Z$ for some $X,Y,Z\subseteq V$ with $X\subseteq Y$.

L239: The $6$ elements of $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{2})$ are $1$, $\alpha_{+}$, $\alpha_{*}$, $\alpha_{+}\alpha_{*}$, $\alpha_{*}\alpha_{+}$, and $\alpha_{+}\alpha_{*}\alpha_{+}$. L261:  | $$d(x,z)=d_{\tau}(x,z)=\ell(p_{x})+\ell(p_{z}),$$  |
L262:  | $$d(y,z)=d_{\tau}(y,z)=\ell(p_{y})+\ell(p_{z}).$$  |

L264: Consequently,
L265: 
L266:  | $$d(x,y,z)=\frac{d(x,y)+d(x,z)-d(y,z)}{2}=\ell(p_{x}).$$  |

L269: ###### Lemma 4.2.
L270: 
L271: For any finite pseudometric space $X$, the following three conditions are equivalent:
L272: 
L273: (i) $c(X)=\{pt\}$;
L274: 
L275: (ii) $X$ is the leaf space of a finite rooted tree;
L276: 
L277: (iii) $\operatorname{card}(X)=1$ or $X$ is the leaf space of a finite non-rooted tree.

If the degree of $\ast$ is $\neq 1$, then the leaf spaces of $\tau$ viewed as a rooted tree and a non-rooted tree coincide and we get (iii). If $\ast$ has degree 1, then $\ast$ is adjacent to a unique edge $e$ connecting $\ast$ to another vertex, $v$, of $\tau$.

If $v$ has degree $\geq 2$, then $X$ is the leaf space of the rooted tree obtained from $\tau$ by deleting $\ast$ and $e$ and taking $v$ for the root. This new rooted tree has less edges than $\tau$ and the implication (ii) $\Longrightarrow$ (iii) follows by induction.

L338: 
L339: Let $\zeta$ be a metric forest whose base $B$ is a trim metric space with $\geq 2$ points. Then at least one of the following two claims hold:
L340: 
L341: (i) the leaf space $\partial\zeta=(\partial\zeta,d_{\zeta})$ of $\zeta$ is obtained from $B$ by a drift;
L342: 
L343: (ii) there is a metric forest with less edges than $\zeta$, same base $B$ as $\zeta$ and the leaf space $\partial\zeta$ or $t(\partial\zeta)$.
L344: ###### Proof.
L345: 
L346: Denote by $|\zeta|$ the number of edges of $\zeta$. The definition of a metric forest implies that $|\zeta|\geq\operatorname{card}(B)$. If $|\zeta|=\operatorname{card}(B)$, then each tree $\zeta_{a}$ with $a\in B$ is just an edge with two vertices (one of them being the root) and a certain length $f(a)\geq 0$. This defines a function $f:B\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $\partial\zeta=B^{f}$. So, (i) holds.
L347: We say that a metric forest is reduced if all its components are reduced rooted trees having no edges of length zero with both endpoints of degree $\neq 1$. If $\zeta$ is not reduced, then eliminating vertices of degree 2 and contracting edges as in the proof of Lemma cite47†4.2 , we obtain a metric forest satisfying (ii).
L348: It remains to prove (ii) in the case where $|\zeta|>\operatorname{card}(B)$ and $\zeta$ is reduced. Since all components of $\zeta$ are reduced, Lemma cite48†5.2 implies that the pseudometric space $(\partial\zeta,d^{\bullet})$ (where $d=d_{\zeta}$) is the leaf space of the metric forest $\zeta^{\bullet}$ obtained from $\zeta$ by changing to zero the lengths of all edges adjacent to leaves. Since $\zeta$ is reduced, the lengths of all other edges of $\zeta^{\bullet}$ are non-zero.
L349: This implies that two distinct leaves $u,v$ of $\zeta$ are related by the equivalence relation $\sim_{d^{\bullet}}$ (i.e., satisfy $d^{\bullet}(u,v)=0$) if and only if they are contiguous leaves of a tree component of $\zeta$.
L350: Then the metric space $t(\partial\zeta,d_{\zeta})=(\widetilde{\partial\zeta},\widetilde{d^{\bullet}})$ is the leaf space of the metric forest $\zeta^{\prime}$ obtained from $\zeta^{\bullet}$ by deleting all but one vertices (and the adjacent edges) in each equivalence class of leaves. To check that $|\zeta^{\prime}|<|\zeta|$, it suffices to note that the equivalence relation $\sim_{d^{\bullet}}$ in $\partial\zeta$ is non-trivial.

L358: ### 5.3. Proof of Theorem cite34†1.5 .
L359: We first prove the transitivity of the relation $\geq$ between finite pseudometric spaces (cf. the introduction). Consider metric forests $\zeta=\{\zeta_{a}\}_{a\in A}$ and $\eta=\{\eta_{b}\}_{b\in B}$ with bases $A$ and $B$ respectively. We claim that if $A=\partial\eta$, then $\partial\zeta\geq B$. To see it, for each $b\in B$ glue the trees $\eta_{b}$ and $\{\zeta_{a}\}_{a}$ where $a\in A$ runs over the leaves of $\eta_{b}$.
L360: The gluing goes by identifying each such $a$ with the root of $\zeta_{a}$ and produces a tree $\mu_{b}$. We take the root of $\eta_{b}$ as the root of $\mu_{b}$. Clearly, the metric forest $\{\mu_{b}\}_{b\in B}$ has the same leaf space as $\zeta$. Hence, $\partial\zeta\geq B$.
L361: To prove Theorem cite34†1.5 , consider a metric forest $\zeta$ with base $A$. Then $\partial\zeta\geq A$ and, by Theorem cite31†1.2 , $A\geq c(A)$. Therefore $\partial\zeta\geq c(A)$, so that there is a metric forest with leaf space $\partial\zeta$ and base $c(A)$. Since $c(A)$ is trim, Theorem cite32†1.3 implies that $c(\partial\zeta)=c(A)$. Thus, $\partial\zeta$ is trim equivalent to $A$.
